hpre-01-c3.text: Wessex Archaeology. The Amesbury Archer. Wessex Archaeology.
hpre-01-c3.quote: came from a colder climate region than we find in Britain today, possibly from some where in central Europe
hpre-01-c3.claim: Isotopes indicate that the "Amesbury Archer", buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BCE, probably spent his childhood in central Europe, perhaps the Alps region.

hpre-02-c2.text: Emma Groeneveld (2017). Early Human Migration. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-02-c2.quote: already by 53,000 years ago, descendants of that main wave out of Africa reached the north of Australia
hpre-02-c2.claim: People had reached Australia by at least about 50,000 years ago, and probably earlier.

hpre-06-c2.text: Joshua J. Mark (2023). Ancient Britain. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-06-c2.quote: according to recent studies (2020), may have at first been turned into several islands before rising sea levels sank them as well
hpre-06-c2.claim: a 2020 study argues that parts of Doggerland survived it as an archipelago for some time.

hpre-03-c1.text: Bruce Bower (2018). Ancient climate shifts may have sparked human ingenuity and networking. Science News.
hpre-03-c1.quote: A substantial number of Olorgesailie’s Middle Stone Age tools are made from obsidian that came from at least 25 to 50 kilometers away from the excavation sites.
hpre-03-c1.claim: At Olorgesailie in Kenya, around 300,000 years ago, people used obsidian from sources 25 to 50 kilometers away

hpre-03-c2.quote: In 2017 their most intriguing discoveries came from a grave containing two adolescent boys who had been buried head to head. This grave held more than 10,000 beads and 16 spears made of mammoth ivory
hpre-03-c2.claim: two boys laid head to head with more than 10,000 beads

hpre-03-c2.quote: Analysis of the skeletons shows that both boys suffered from physical abnormalities. One boy had severely shortened and bowed leg bones.
hpre-03-c2.claim: one boy had exceptionally short, bowed thigh bones.

hpre-04-c1.text: Ronnie Jones III (2015). Göbekli Tepe. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-04-c1.quote: As excavator Klaus Schmidt put it, "First came the temple, then the city."
hpre-04-c1.claim: Schmidt called the site the world's first temple, a ritual center where mobile hunter-gatherers gathered for feasts, and summed up his view as "first came the temple, then the city".

hpre-04-c3.text: Nathalie Choubineh (2021). Çatalhöyük. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-04-c3.quote: Bone analyses of the buried skeletons in Çatalhöyük indicate equal diets and equal workloads for men and women.
hpre-04-c3.claim: isotope studies suggested that men and women ate similar diets.

hpre-05-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2026). Sumerian King List: Who Was King? And Who Was Not King?. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-05-c1.quote: The most complete version of the Sumerian King List is the Weld-Blundell Prism (circa 1800 BCE), discovered in the ruins of ancient Larsa in 1922.
hpre-05-c1.claim: the best preserved, the Weld-Blundell Prism, dates to about 1800 BCE.

hpre-05-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2026). Sumerian King List: Who Was King? And Who Was Not King?. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-05-c1.quote: In Eridu, Alulim became king; he ruled for 28,800 years.
hpre-05-c1.claim: Alulim of Eridu reigned 28,800 years; En-men-lu-ana of Bad-tibira, 43,200.

hpre-05-c3.text: Joshua J. Mark (2026). Gilgamesh: The Historical and Mythical King. World History Encyclopedia.
hpre-05-c3.quote: Accordingly, Gilgamesh was a demigod, who was said to have lived an exceptionally long life (the Sumerian King List records his reign as 126 years) and to have possessed superhuman strength.
hpre-05-c3.claim: Gilgamesh appears as the fifth king of Uruk, "whose father was a phantom", ruling 126 years.
